triples.relationship: Thematic contrast: cattle fertility and the prosperity of the ungodly
triples.rationale: Job points to successful animal reproduction among the ungodly whose prosperity troubles him. Deuteronomy includes flourishing herds and freedom from barrenness among the blessings associated with keeping the covenant. The comparison places Job's observation beside that blessing pattern without treating prosperity as proof of obedience or equating freedom from barrenness with the precise absence of miscarriage.
triples.source_text: Their cow did not calve prematurely; their pregnant animal was preserved and did not miscarry.

target_units.text: And it shall be, when you hearken unto all these ordinances, and keep and do them, that the Lord your God shall keep with you the covenant and the mercy which He sware unto your fathers.

And He shall love you, and bless you, and multiply you; and He shall bless the offspring of your womb, and the fruit of your land, your grain, and your wine, and your oil, the herds of your cattle and the flocks of your sheep, upon the land which the Lord sware unto your fathers to give you.
You shall be blessed above all the nations; there shall be no barren male or female among you, nor among your cattle.

triples.relationship: Imagery comparison: playing children as a picture of well-being
triples.rationale: Job includes playing children in the secure, prosperous households of the ungodly. Zechariah pictures Jerusalem restored with elderly residents and boys and girls playing in its squares. The shared image makes well-being visible through children's play, while Job's troubling example and Zechariah's promised restoration have different moral and narrative settings.
triples.source_text: They remain like everlasting sheep, and their children play,

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord Almighty: Old men and old women will again sit in Jerusalem’s squares, each holding a staff in hand because of many days.
The city’s squares will be filled with boys and girls playing in her squares.

triples.relationship: Ethical comparison: the condemnation of partiality
triples.rationale: Eliphaz accuses Job of favoring particular people and settling them on the land. Leviticus forbids favoring the poor or admiring the mighty in judgment and requires righteous treatment of a neighbor. The link concerns condemned favoritism; it neither establishes a particular land grant nor endorses Eliphaz's accusation against Job.
triples.source_text: You showed partiality to certain people and settled them upon the land.

target_units.text: You shall do no injustice in judgment; you shall not favour the person of the poor, neither shall you admire the person of the mighty; you shall judge your neighbour in righteousness.

triples.relationship: Imagery contrast: enduring paths distinguished by their moral character
triples.rationale: Eliphaz asks whether Job will keep the age-old path trodden by unjust men. Jeremiah directs hearers to ask for the Lord's eternal paths, discern the good way and walk in it. Both use an enduring path as an image for a chosen course of conduct, but the unjust path and the Lord's good way are explicitly contrasted rather than identified.
triples.source_text: Will you guard the age-old path that unjust men trod,

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Stand upon the roads and see, and ask for the Lord’s eternal paths and see which is the good way, and walk in it, and you will find purification for your souls. And they said, ‘We will not go.’

triples.relationship: Imagery parallel: clapping and hissing at a downfall
triples.rationale: The ending of Job's description of the ungodly person's fate combines clapping hands and hissing him out of his place. Passersby in Lamentations likewise clap and hiss at fallen Jerusalem. The particular pairing expresses derision at a downfall; the comparison does not identify the unnamed actor in Job or equate the individual with Jerusalem.
triples.source_text: He will clap his hands over him and hiss him out of his place.”

target_units.text: All who pass along the road clapped their hands at you. They hissed and shook their heads at Daughter Jerusalem: “Is this the city they will call a crown of glory, the gladness of all the earth?”

triples.relationship: Material comparison: processing precious metals in wisdom teaching
triples.rationale: Job distinguishes the known sources of silver and the place where gold is filtered before asking where wisdom can be found. Proverbs draws on the testing of silver and gold in a furnace to describe the choosing of hearts before the Lord. Both use the handling of precious metals within wisdom teaching, while filtering, testing and the lessons drawn from them remain distinct.
triples.source_text: “For silver has a place from which it comes, and gold a place from which it is filtered.

target_units.text: As silver and gold are tested in a furnace, so hearts are chosen before the Lord.

triples.relationship: Material parallel: iron and copper obtained from the land
triples.rationale: Job says that iron comes from earth and copper is quarried like stone. Deuteronomy describes the good land's stones as iron and copper mined from its hills. Both explicitly associate these two metals with extraction from the earth; Job's statement does not identify his location with the promised land.
triples.source_text: For iron comes from earth, and copper is quarried like stone.

target_units.text: a land wherein you shall eat your bread without poverty, and shall lack nothing; a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills you shall mine copper.

triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: God's observation extends everywhere
triples.rationale: The wisdom poem explains God's knowledge by His observation of the entire realm under heaven and everything in the earth He made. Proverbs likewise places the Lord's eyes everywhere, observing evil and good people. Both stress the unrestricted extent of divine observation, with Job emphasizing creation and Proverbs the people within it.
triples.source_text: For He observes the whole realm under heaven, knowing everything in the earth that He made:

target_units.text: The eyes of the Lord are in every place; they observe both evil people and good people.

triples.relationship: Imagery parallel: breaking teeth as the overthrow of predatory injustice
triples.rationale: Job describes rescuing plunder by crushing unjust people's molars and tearing it from their teeth. The psalm, after describing lawless people, says that God shattered their teeth and crushed the lions' grinders. Both portray the defeat of harmful power through broken teeth; Job's claim of defending victims is distinct from the psalm's attribution of the act to God.
triples.source_text: I crushed the molars of unjust people and tore the plunder from between their teeth.

target_units.text: God shattered their teeth in their mouth; the Lord crushed the lions’ grinders.

triples.relationship: Verbal parallel: a discredited name extinguished
triples.rationale: Job describes the foolish and dishonored people connected with his mockers as having their name and renown extinguished from the earth. Proverbs contrasts praised righteous memory with the extinguished name of the impious. The shared image is the extinction of a discredited name; the proverb is not used to verify Job's assessment of the particular people he describes.
triples.source_text: sons of foolish and dishonored people, whose name and renown were extinguished from the earth.

target_units.text: The memory of righteous people is with praises, but the name of the impious is extinguished.

triples.relationship: Ethical parallel: refusing the company and paths of wrongdoing
triples.rationale: Job's conditional oath rejects walking with mockers and hurrying toward deceit. The psalm blesses the person who does not walk in ungodly counsel, stand in sinners' way or sit with pestilent men. Both express moral separation through movement and company; the psalm's supplied term pestilent men is not replaced with mockers, and the two passages' particular offenses remain distinct.
triples.source_text: If I had walked with mockers, and if my foot also hastened toward deceit,

target_units.text: Blessed is the man who did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, and did not stand in the way of sinners, and did not sit in the seat of pestilent men;

triples.relationship: Wisdom comparison: restraint in a younger person's speech
triples.rationale: Elihu explains that his youth in relation to the others made him remain silent before offering his knowledge. Sirach gives elders an appropriate speaking role and counsels a young man to speak when needed, briefly, without claiming equality among dignitaries or interrupting another. Both connect age and restraint in speech, while the debate and banquet settings differ and Sirach does not endorse Elihu's subsequent arguments.
triples.source_text: Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite replied: “I am younger in time, and you are older; therefore I kept quiet, afraid to announce my own knowledge to you.

target_units.text: Speak, elder, for it is fitting for you, with exact knowledge, but do not hinder the music.
Where there is a performance, do not pour out chatter or display wisdom at an unsuitable time.
A carbuncle signet upon a golden ornament—so is an ensemble of musicians at a wine banquet.
An emerald signet in a gold setting—so is musicians’ melody with pleasant wine.
Speak, young man, if you are needed; scarcely twice, if you are asked.
Sum up your speech, much in few words; be like someone who knows and at the same time keeps silent.
Among dignitaries do not make yourself their equal, and while another speaks do not chatter much.

triples.relationship: Illustrative parallel: fear arising through a revelatory dream
triples.rationale: In Elihu's account, God uses a fearful dream or nighttime meditation to uncover people's minds and turn them away from injustice. Nebuchadnezzar reports that a dream made him apprehensive and that fear fell upon him; its interpretation later warns him about divine judgment and urges reform. The king's experience illustrates this fear-and-warning pattern without making him the unnamed person in Elihu's description.
triples.source_text: then He uncovers people’s minds; with such forms of fear He terrified them,

target_units.text: In the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, he said, “I was at peace in my house and prospering upon my throne.
I saw a dream and became apprehensive; fear fell upon me.

triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: acknowledging fault to another in a context of restoration
triples.rationale: Elihu's conditional account includes turning toward the Lord and announcing one's own blame to a human before the restoration described next. James connects forgiveness and healing with prayer and confession of sins to one another. The comparison concerns interpersonal acknowledgment of fault amid hoped-for restoration; it does not replace Job's death-bearing angels with an interpreter or equate its unusual surrounding clauses with James's instructions.
triples.source_text: If there are a thousand death-bearing angels, one of them will certainly not wound him. If he understands in his heart to turn toward the Lord, announces his own blame to a human, and shows his lack of understanding,

target_units.text: And the prayer of faith will save the weary sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.
Therefore confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be healed. A righteous person’s petition has great strength when it is at work.

triples.relationship: Thematic parallel: rejection of divine law associated with injustice and judgment
triples.rationale: Elihu attributes the ungodly people's destruction to turning aside from God's law, in a context of the needy crying out. Isaiah likewise joins corrupt judgment against the righteous with consuming judgment because the people did not desire the Lord's law and provoked His utterance. Both connect injustice, rejection of divine instruction and judgment; Isaiah's oracle is not treated as direct confirmation of every claim in Elihu's speech.
triples.source_text: because they turned aside from God’s law and did not recognize His ordinances,

target_units.text: who justify the ungodly for gifts and take away the righteous person’s right!

Therefore, as a stalk is burned by a fiery coal and consumed by a rising flame, their root will become like chaff and their blossom rise like dust. For they did not desire the law of the Lord Sabaoth, but provoked the utterance of the Holy One of Israel.

triples.relationship: Wisdom comparison: righteousness and wisdom directed toward other people
triples.rationale: Elihu contrasts the inability to enrich God with human conduct directed toward fellow humans, saying that one's righteousness is for a son of humanity. Proverbs says that becoming wise for oneself also makes one wise for one's neighbors. Both direct attention to the human beneficiaries of right conduct or wisdom; Proverbs' further statement about bearing one's own evils is not made identical to Elihu's wording about ungodliness.
triples.source_text: Your ungodliness is for a man like you, and your righteousness for a son of humanity.

target_units.text: Son, if you become wise for yourself, you will also be wise for your neighbors; but if you turn out evil, you alone will bear evils.

deferred_source_units.source_text: They unjustly lay in ambush in narrow places and did not know a righteous road.
deferred_source_units.reason: The fresh Proverbs 1:11-16 lead was read in its actual native wording. It speaks of hiding a righteous man in the earth, taking property and avoiding the criminals' paths, but does not explicitly describe an ambush in narrow places. A connection resting only on the general metaphor of a wicked road was not retained; Job's native ambush wording remains intact.

deferred_source_units.source_text: The abyss said, ‘It is not in me,’ and the sea said, ‘It is not with me.’
deferred_source_units.reason: Deuteronomy 30:11-14 was read as a possible sea-and-instruction comparison. Its command is not across the sea and is near the hearer, whereas Job personifies the abyss and sea as denying possession of wisdom. The remaining shared sea imagery was insufficient for a particular retained relationship; the texts' different claims were not merged.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: They unjustly lay in ambush in narrow places and did not know a righteous road.
unresolved_candidates.reason: Job explicitly describes an unjust ambush in narrow places and ignorance of a righteous road. The native Proverbs text instead describes hiding a righteous man in the earth, seizing his property, and refusing the criminals' paths. It was not rewritten as an ambush proposal; the general violent-path association alone was not retained.

target_units.text: Come with us; share in bloodshed. Let us hide a righteous man in the earth unjustly;
let us swallow him alive like Hades and remove his memory from the earth.
Let us seize his costly property and fill our houses with spoils.
Cast your lot among us; let us all obtain a common purse, and let there be one moneybag for us.
Do not walk in the way with them; turn your foot away from their paths,
for their feet run toward evil, and they are quick to shed blood.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: The abyss said, ‘It is not in me,’ and the sea said, ‘It is not with me.’
unresolved_candidates.reason: The sea in Job denies that wisdom is with it. Deuteronomy says its command is not across the sea and is instead near the hearer. These concern different spatial claims and different subjects; shared sea imagery and the general question of instruction were not sufficient to retain a pair.

target_units.text: For this commandment which I command you this day is not excessively burdensome, neither is it far from you.
It is not in heaven above, that you should say, Who shall ascend for us into heaven, and fetch it for us, that we may hear it and do it?
Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, Who shall cross for us unto the other side of the sea, and fetch it for us, and make us hear it, that we may do it?
The word is very near you, in your mouth, and in your heart, and in your hands, that you may do it.
